article.title: PyPI, Packagist and GitHub Lock Different Parts of a Published Release, GitHub's Only Where Enabled: A Comparison With Four 2026 Incidents
article.summary: The Herald compares PyPI's 14-day limit on new files, Packagist's locked stable-version references and GitHub's opt-in immutable releases with four 2026 incidents it selected; in its reading, the rules cover different ground.
article.body_markdown:
## Background

Four supply-chain incidents reported between March and October 2026 involved release tags, release files or newly uploaded versions: two moved git tags, one swapped files on existing GitHub releases, and one uploaded new versions to PyPI with stolen credentials. The four are the Herald's own selection of cases that bear on how a published release can change; they are not a count of all such incidents. Three of the platforms involved, PyPI, Packagist and GitHub, now have rules limiting changes to published releases. The Herald's reading, set out and labelled under Implications, is that the three rules lock different objects and that none of them, as described in the cited sources, addresses a new version published with stolen credentials. The Herald covered these incidents separately, including [the Trivy action tags](/article/2026-03/24-trivy-supply-chain-attack-escalates-as-teampcp-hijacks-75-github-action-tags-defaced-aqua-security-repositories-and-spreads-to-npm), [the Laravel-Lang tag rewrites](/article/2026-05/24-laravel-lang-supply-chain-attack-poisons-over-700-package-versions-via-packagist-tag-hijack-deploying-cross-platform-credential-stealer) and [the OVHcloud CLI release swap](/article/2026-10/20-ovhcloud-cli-releases-hijacked-through-a-contributors-github-account-with-swapped-binaries-live-for-up-to-94-minutes).

**Trivy action tags, reported March 20.** [The Hacker News](https://thehackernews.com/2026/03/trivy-security-scanner-github-actions.html) quoted Socket researcher Philipp Burckhardt as saying an attacker "force-pushed 75 out of 76 version tags in the aquasecurity/trivy-action repository". The same article says Aqua Security counted 76 of 77 tags, and it quotes Socket as saying Aqua's advisory counts all tag names, including duplicates, which explains the difference. [LWN](https://lwn.net/Articles/1064693/) describes the mechanism: "a large number of release tags were force-pushed to point to the new commits". LWN adds that the attacker worked "without changing any existing branches, avoiding the notifications that would have normally gone out in response to such changes."

**LiteLLM, March 24.** According to [LWN](https://lwn.net/Articles/1064693/), LiteLLM was one of the projects caught by the Trivy compromise: the PyPI credentials of one of its developers were harvested and then used to upload compromised versions 1.82.7 and 1.82.8 to PyPI, and "the word went out" on March 24.

**Laravel-Lang, May 22 and 23.** [BleepingComputer](https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/laravel-lang-packages-hijacked-to-deploy-credential-stealing-malware/) reported that attackers rewrote GitHub tags across four Laravel Lang repositories "rather than publishing entirely new malicious versions", and [The Hacker News](https://thehackernews.com/2026/05/laravel-lang-php-packages-compromised.html) states that the attackers "rewrote every existing git tag in each repository". Both outlets draw on security firms (StepSecurity, Aikido and Socket). BleepingComputer quotes StepSecurity as saying the rewrites started at 22:32 UTC and finished by 00:00 UTC, and The Hacker News quotes Socket putting the tags on May 22 and May 23. The firms' counts differ: BleepingComputer reports Aikido at 233 versions across three repositories and Socket at roughly 700 historical versions, while The Hacker News reports more than 700 versions identified; neither outlet reconciles the figures. The Hacker News also quotes Socket describing "newly published tags" appearing in rapid succession, a wording it does not reconcile with its own "rewrote" description; this article uses the rewrite description that both outlets carry.

**OVHcloud CLI, October 19.** [The Hacker News](https://thehackernews.com/2026/10/hackers-hijack-five-ovhcloud-cli.html) reports that an attacker used a contributor's GitHub account to replace the download archives on five existing releases, v0.11.0 through v0.15.0, which were published between April 14 and September 16. The swapped files were live "from 12:47 to 14:21 UTC", and the report says the source code, the release tag and the build pipeline were not touched. The same outlet explains why this was possible: anyone with write access can delete the files attached to a release and upload new ones with the same names, and "the download URL does not change unless release immutability is enabled". It reports that OVHcloud had not enabled that setting. The report attributes the contributor-account details and a timeline to OpenSourceMalware, which investigated the incident, so within the sources cited here the OVHcloud case rests on a single outlet.

**Sourcing in this comparison.** The Trivy case rests on The Hacker News and LWN; LiteLLM on LWN; Laravel-Lang on BleepingComputer and The Hacker News, both relaying security-firm research; OVHcloud on The Hacker News. The PyPI rule rests on PyPI's code and issue plus two items that restate its announcement, an LWN brief and an entry in a Hacker News weekly roundup; the Packagist rule on its own repository, with no cited outlet covering it; GitHub's feature on GitHub's changelog and documentation plus The Hacker News's description.

## Current situation

### PyPI: no new files on releases older than 14 days

A pull request to PyPI's Warehouse codebase, [merged on July 8 at 21:43 UTC](https://github.com/pypi/warehouse/pull/19727) by GitHub's timestamp, makes uploads of new files to older releases fail. The code at the [merge commit](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/pypi/warehouse/e0ee5f839d7568bba2d8ef170b5601abdfa3da14/warehouse/forklift/legacy.py) sets the limit at 14 days, compares it with the release's creation time and answers with an error saying that uploading new files to releases older than 14 days is not allowed. A comment in that code says the feature "explicitly doesn't protect against users deleting and recreating releases in the UI, only against uploads through compromised API tokens or workflows". The [issue it closes](https://github.com/pypi/warehouse/issues/19726), opened on March 24, states the threat as "they can publish new artifacts to existing releases".

Two outlet items cover the rule, and both restate PyPI's announcement rather than reporting independently. [LWN's July 22 brief](https://lwn.net/Articles/1084218/) relays the announcement by Python Software Foundation security developer-in-residence Seth Larson and its figures: the discussion "was restarted in March 2026 after the popular packages LiteLLM and Telnyx were compromised", and a query of the top 15,000 packages found "only 56 projects of 15,000" had published a Python 3.14-compatible wheel more than 14 days after a release was available. [The Hacker News's July 23 ThreatsDay roundup](https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/threatsday-android-spyware-plc-attacks.html) carries a short item that quotes PyPI as saying: "As far as we are aware, this has not yet been abused, but there is no technical reason beyond that attackers weren't aware it was possible."

### Packagist: stable versions keep their original reference

A [Packagist pull request](https://github.com/composer/packagist/pull/1742) opened on May 27 and merged on June 5 at 06:52 UTC (GitHub timestamps) makes stable versions immutable. Its text gives its reason: the updater "silently rewrites a stable version row whenever upstream changes the source/dist reference", while "downstream lock files, mirrors, and security scanners all assume a tagged release is a frozen snapshot". The project's [documentation template](https://github.com/composer/packagist/blob/main/templates/about/version_immutability.html.twig) says the source and dist reference of a published stable version are locked even if the upstream tag is moved or rewritten, that dev branches keep tracking their branches, and that a maintainer who needs a fix should tag a new version such as 1.2.4 or 1.2.3.1. A detected re-tag produces a warning, a maintainer email, an audit record and a badge on the version page. Neither its text nor its review comments mention an incident, and the cited sources give the merge date but no production deploy date; the author's one general comment, on June 4, said the change was ready and "will deploy it tomorrow morning". None of the outlet articles cited in this piece mentions the rule.

### GitHub: immutable releases, where enabled

[GitHub's October 28, 2025 changelog](https://github.blog/changelog/2025-10-28-immutable-releases-are-now-generally-available/) made immutable releases generally available as a setting that can be enabled "at the repository or organization level". Once it is on, "All new releases are immutable", while "Existing releases remain mutable unless you republish them." [GitHub's documentation](https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/concepts/supply-chain-security/immutable-releases) says an immutable release's tag cannot be moved and its assets cannot be modified or deleted, while the title and release notes stay editable. After the swap, OVHcloud published v0.16.0 as an immutable release, according to The Hacker News.

On the consumer side, GitHub's [October 28, 2026 changelog](https://github.blog/changelog/2026-10-28-github-actions-workflow-lockfiles-are-generally-available/) made workflow lockfiles generally available: they "let you keep readable tag and branch references in your workflows while running the exact commits you locked, even if those references move". The same changelog cautions that lockfiles "don’t determine whether a dependency is safe." In the Trivy report, Wiz researcher Rami McCarthy is quoted advising "Pin GitHub Actions to full SHA hashes, not version tags". In the OVHcloud case, The Hacker News says a customer's CI job caught the swap because it pinned the SHA-256 of one archive, and that a Homebrew cask that pinned each archive's hash would have refused the swapped files.

## Implications

The comparison below is the Herald's own reading of the sources above, not a finding of any of them.

**The rules name different objects.** Sorted by what changed, two incidents moved git tags (Trivy, Laravel-Lang), one replaced files attached to existing releases (OVHcloud) and one uploaded new versions (LiteLLM). Packagist's rule names the reference behind a stable version, which is where a tag rewrite acts. GitHub's names a release's tag and assets, and only for releases made after a maintainer enables it; the cited sources do not say whether the tags moved in the Trivy and Laravel-Lang cases belonged to immutable releases. PyPI's names new files on releases older than 14 days. None of the three rules, as described in these sources, stops a new version being published with stolen credentials, which is the LiteLLM pattern. The cited sources also describe no case of files being added to an older PyPI release: the PyPI issue presents that as a threat, and PyPI is quoted by The Hacker News as saying it was not aware of abuse. LWN relays a figure of 56 of the top 15,000 projects for late Python 3.14 wheels.

**One case has a documented unused control.** For OVHcloud, The Hacker News reports that the option had been available since October 2025 and was not enabled. None of the cited sources reports how many projects have enabled the setting. Whether a platform-wide rule or an opt-in suits this problem better is a question the sources do not settle: GitHub's setting protects only releases created after it is turned on, while the PyPI and Packagist rules are changes to the registries' own code, with no per-project setting described.

**Detection and notification differ across the cases.** LWN notes that, in the Trivy case, moving tags avoided the notifications a branch change would have triggered. Packagist's documentation lists an email and an audit record for a blocked re-tag. In the OVHcloud case, the swap surfaced because a customer's pinned hash stopped matching. Lockfiles and hash pins place the check with the consumer, while the three rules place it with the registry or the publisher; the sources describe both, and none of them compares the two.

**What the sources leave open.** The Packagist template names a reference, not archive contents, and none of the cited sources says whether the downloaded archives themselves are locked. The PyPI comment says its rule does not cover deleting and recreating a release in the web interface. The two disagreements among the sources differ in kind: the Trivy count difference (75 of 76 versus 76 of 77) is explained in The Hacker News by a duplicated tag name, while the Laravel-Lang counts (233 versus roughly 700) are not reconciled in the cited articles, so those figures are best read per source. As of November 15, 2026, none of the cited sources reports a case in which any of the three rules blocked a malicious change.

Two of the sources give maintainers publishing guidance: Packagist's template says to publish a new version instead of changing a tagged one, and GitHub's documentation recommends attaching all assets to a draft release before publishing, so that they are in place before the release becomes immutable. Among the measures the cited sources describe for consumers are pinning to commit hashes (Wiz, and Aqua as relayed by The Hacker News), lockfiles (GitHub) and hash pins (the OVHcloud customer and the Homebrew cask).
